_: Every modelling assumption in the cost side, in one place, so each one can
be argued with. Values marked ESTIMATE are judgement, not Omaha figures;
replace them with Omaha bid tabs and asset inventories when you have them.
Everything else is sourced.
Streets and sewers are priced at what they cost to keep up over their
lives, not at what the budget spends on them, so the bases that include
them can show a citywide gap. The most consequential inputs are the
street reconstruction lives and how much sewer renewal is lining rather
than open-cut replacement. Defaults are the middle ('Typical') of the
Low / Typical / High range in config/parameters.json; the map's cost
estimate switches pick between them. Services (police, fire, parks,
general government) are allocated from the 2026 budget and balance by
construction.

projection._: Local planar frame in feet, WGS84 radii evaluated at Omaha's latitude. Good to ~0.2% over a 30 km city, i.e. inches on a 70 ft frontage.

_: General Fund facts from the 2026 adopted budget, used to scale GF
appropriations down to the share property tax actually funds, and to
assert that the levy_cents rows in budget.csv reconcile to the real levy.
Formulation: a parcel boundary is sampled every sample_ft, and each sample
is attributed to the nearest street centerline within max_offset_ft for
that street's class. There is deliberately NO parallelism test: on a
cul-de-sac bulb the lot lines are radial to the arc and a parallelism
filter would zero them out — and west Omaha's cul-de-sacs are exactly the
parcels whose cost allocation carries the argument.
max_offset_ft is half the right-of-way plus a setback tolerance.
Cul-de-sacs need their own rule. The centerline stops in the middle of the
bulb, so every point on a bulb lot's curved front projects onto the same
spot - the end of the line - and a span along the street measures zero.
4,857 houses were charged nothing for streets that way. Beyond a dead end
the model instead measures the angle the lot sweeps around the end of the
line, times the radius of its front line: the length of its curved
frontage. bulb_reach_ft is wider than max_offset_ft because a bulb's
right-of-way radius is wider than half a street.
bulb_centerline_share prices the bulb's pavement, which the centerline
does not include: each foot of bulb frontage adds half a foot of street,
the same ratio as a street with lots on both sides. That keeps cul-de-sac
lots paying the same per foot as everyone else rather than less.
A parcel fronts a street only where no other parcel stands between it and
the street: along each side of each street, a boundary sample is dropped
when another parcel has one within occlude_window_ft of it along the street
and more than occlude_depth_ft closer. Arterial reach is wide enough that
the lots behind a corner lot otherwise took shares of its side street.
The window is a little over half the sample spacing, so a fronting lot
always has a sample in it.
A lot line nearer the centerline than occlude_min_ft would be in the
pavement: the centerline is drawn off the street there (Sprague St near
96th runs ~40 ft into the north row), so such a line hides nothing.
Dwelling units: address points are a real unit count for houses, duplexes and
small multifamily, but NOT for apartment complexes. Two separate problems:
(a) DOGIS averages only 2.8 address points across parcels the assessor calls
'Multiple Comm', so a 200-unit tower would read as three dwellings.
(b) BLDG_SF is the floor area of BUILDING #1 ONLY. 12% of multi-family
parcels have more than one building and one has 214 - a 37-acre garden
complex was reading as 35 units at $1.6M apiece.
So multi-family units come from BLDG_SF x NUMBLDGS instead. sf_per_dwelling is
1250 rather than a true 900 gross sf/unit because NUMBLDGS also counts garages,
clubhouses and maintenance sheds; the inflated divisor absorbs them. That lands
at ~208,600 total dwellings against a census count near 216,000, which is the
check that this is calibrated rather than invented. Address points count only
where the assessor has a building: vacant lots and the land-only strips beside
row houses carry points too.
Household size is split by tenure. Applying the citywide 2.42 average to
apartments overstated their population by about 17% and understated
single-family by about 8% - and since 53% of allocated cost is people-driven,
that error landed directly on the density comparison.
Employees are floor area over a per-account-type intensity. Exempt institutions
are included on purpose: a hospital or university employs thousands and
generates police, fire and street demand accordingly.

dwelling._: multi_family units = BLDG_SF x max(NUMBLDGS,1) / sf_per_dwelling

_: What the existing street network costs a year to keep, independent of
what the budget spends on it. Pavement is renewal: rebuild cost over its
life plus resurfacing cost over its interval, per lane-foot. Upkeep is
the city's actual 2026 operating spend, spread per lane-foot. Bridges
and signals are replacement cost over life. Unit costs are 2026 dollars
anchored on Omaha bids and capital-plan estimates; values marked
ESTIMATE are judgement between those anchors, and the reconstruction
lives are the softest inputs in the model.
The network is Public Works' own inventory (DOGIS
Streets_For_Public_Works_CCSM), which carries lane counts. Divided roads
are drawn once per direction with that direction's lanes, so pricing by
the lane-foot counts each carriageway once.

surface_kind._: Public Works surface_type codes. 'none': unimproved or substandard streets, which abutting owners pay to bring up to standard (OMC 26-47), so the city carries upkeep but no renewal.

_: Full-depth reconstruction, all-in, per lane-foot. Local: 183rd St & Wright
St concrete reconstruction bid, $1,599,850 over ~0.67 mi = $452/ft for
two lanes, plus ~20% engineering and contingency (City Clerk agenda
2026-04-21). Minor arterial: 84th St Harrison to L, $14.0M over 1.5 mi
= $1,770/ft for five lanes (2026 CIP, DOGIS PW_CIP_Project_Lines).
Collector and major arterial are ESTIMATE between and beyond those.

reconstruct_life_years._: ESTIMATE, the middle of a range. Years between full rebuilds, with resurfacing in between. Well-maintained city streets average 50-60 years (Golden Valley MN pavement policy); Omaha still runs 1950s-70s concrete with panel repair and overlays. Low 80/70/60, High 50/45/40 in config/parameters.json.

overlay._: Mill and overlay, all-in: 2025 program $28.6M for 150+ lane-miles = ~$191K per lane-mile (KIOS, 2025-02-26). 2026 contract bids alone run $122-148K per lane-mile.

concrete._: Concrete panel and joint repair: residential area 4510, $1.125M over 7.09 mi = ~$15 per lane-foot; 60th St (4 lanes) $1.46M = ~$61 per lane-foot (2025 bids).

resurface_interval_years._: City maintenance engineer: '15 to 20 years on a residential street resurfacing... Major streets... 8 to 12 years' (WOWT, 2023-03-29). Collector ESTIMATE between.

_: Arterials and collectors carry traffic from across the city, so the
homes lining one should not pay for all of it. With this enabled, a
parcel is charged what its frontage would cost as a two-lane
neighbourhood street, and everything above that - the extra lanes, the
bridges and signals - is pooled and spread over every foot of street
frontage in the city. Disable it to charge each road's full cost to the
parcels that front it.
2026 adopted appropriations for running the street network, spread per
lane-foot. Left out: construction inspection, design and Public Works
administration (overhead of capital projects), park roads, creek
channels, graffiti, and the resurfacing programs, which are renewal and
already in pavement above. Street lighting is OPPD's tariff, which covers
the lights' own capital and maintenance.

bridges._: City-owned structures in the FHWA National Bridge Inventory (owner 04, place 37000), culverts included. FHWA 2025 Bridge Replacement Unit Costs: Nebraska, off the National Highway System, $280/sf (3-year average). AASHTO LRFD design life 75 years.

_: Active signals in DOGIS Noneditable_Signal_Intersections (972, 2026).
ESTIMATE: $300K construction per intersection (Des Moines 2026, $600K
for two; Le Mars IA 2025, $865K for three) plus ~30% for design and the
city-furnished cabinet and controller. Pedestrian signals, hybrid
beacons and the like ESTIMATE at $150K. Life: Omaha's median age at
rebuild is 31 years (same layer).

streets.sidewalks: Not charged. Abutting owners pay to repair sidewalks (OMC 26-41 to 26-44). The city's ADA ramps are built with resurfacing and are in its all-in cost.

_: Money the city puts into streets that is not property tax, from the
2026 adopted budget: the Street Allocation Fund's fuel and wheel taxes,
and the part of the General Fund's street spending (Public Works and
debt service, the rows budget.csv charges by frontage) paid by sales
tax and other non-property revenue, i.e. x (1 - 123,425,531 /
562,783,754). No parcel pays it directly, so it is credited to every
street in proportion to its cost: it covers the same share of every
parcel's street bill. Borrowing is not counted: bonds are repaid from
the debt-service levy, which is already property tax.
Omaha's sewers are an enterprise fund paid by sewer use fees, which M.U.D.
bills on the City's behalf - not by property tax. So sewer is counted on
both sides: each parcel's estimated sewer bill is income, and what its
share of the system costs to keep is cost. Nothing forces the two to
match.
The cost side has two parts. Mains along the lot: renewal and cleaning of
the local mains under the streets the parcel fronts, split by frontage
like streets. Everything else - trunk lines, mains off the street grid,
treatment plants, pump stations, the CSO works, operations - is shared
in proportion to each parcel's sewer bill, i.e. its flow, after scaling
to the city's share of the system's fee revenue.
Fees use the published 2026 residential rates. Water use per property is
not public, so it is estimated: usage values are ESTIMATE. M.U.D.'s own
sample bill assumes 6 CCF a month. Non-residential flow is estimated from
modelled employees. Multi-family complexes are billed per building, not
per unit. Storm and sanitary mains are not distinguished in the source
layer, so both are counted.

fees._: 2026 Omaha sewer use charges, M.U.D. brochure (effective 2026-01-01).

usage_ccf_per_month._: ESTIMATE. 1 CCF = 748 gallons; 1 CCF per employee is ~25 gallons a workday.

_: Renewal is a blend of open-cut replacement and lining from inside
(cured-in-place pipe). Replacement, all-in, dollars per foot = base +
per_inch x diameter: Carollo's 2024 unit cost study for Phoenix (8-inch
$350-400, 24-inch $770-940, 36-inch $1,230-1,550, construction only) plus
~20% engineering, checked against Omaha projects (24th & Ogden storm, Cole
Creek). Life 75 years, inside the 50-100 Omaha's Wastewater Collection
System Design Manual gives gravity pipe. Lining: ESTIMATE $12 per inch of
diameter per foot over 50 years (Lawrence KS 2019 bid: 24-inch CIPP at
$97.75/ft against $700-800 open-cut). lined_percent is the share of
renewal done by lining: ESTIMATE, Low 75 / Typical 50 / High 0.
Priced by diameter because LINE_TYPE is not a size: 'Collector' mains are
8-inch, the smallest public pipe, while 'Sewer' lines run 15-96 inches.
default_diameter_in fills missing diameters with each type's median.
trunk_types carry flow from whole basins, so they are shared like
treatment rather than charged to the street above. So is any main wider
than local_max_diameter_in (ESTIMATE): local sanitary collectors are 8-12
inches and storm laterals 15-18; past that a pipe drains a neighbourhood
or a watershed, not the block it runs under.

pipe_upkeep._: 2026 adopted: sewer cleaning and repair of mains, manholes and inlets, spread per foot of city-owned main.

operations._: 2026 adopted Sewer Revenue operating costs other than main cleaning. Systemwide; scaled to the city's share. Flood control (levees and their pump stations) is left out: it is paid by the separate storm water fee, which is not counted as income either.

_: Replacement value over life for what is not in the pipe inventory.
Omaha publishes no replacement values, so all three are ESTIMATES built
from sourced unit costs. Plants: 46 + 95 MGD max-month design (HDR,
2024) is ~118 MGD average-day, at ~$13.5M per MGD (Tomahawk Creek, KS,
2020, $14.1M/MGD, escalated and scaled for size), over a 40-year blended
life (structures 50, equipment 20-25). Pump stations: ~51 sewer stations
(the design manual's ~70 less 19 flood-control ones); the nine CSO lift
stations at Omaha's own cost per MGD, the rest at ~$2.5M each (Carollo
2024, EPA needs-survey curve), 33-year blended life. CSO works: only the
assets not already counted as pipe, plant or pump station - Saddle Creek
retention basin ($142M), South Interceptor Force Main ($54M), controls
and green infrastructure (~$20M) - escalated 1.2x, 42-year life. Sewer
fund depreciation for comparison: $61.5M (FY2025 ACFR, historical cost).

groups.title: Street pavement
groups.what: Rebuilding and resurfacing every street the City maintains: 2,212 miles, 5,064 lane-miles.
groups.how: Per lane-foot, per year: the rebuild cost divided by the years it lasts, plus the resurfacing cost divided by the years between resurfacings. A parcel pays for its share of the lane-feet in front of it; a lot with lots across the street pays for half.

about.text: Asphalt and asphalt-over-concrete streets get an overlay; bare concrete gets panel and joint repair instead. Unimproved streets get no rebuild, because their owners pay to bring them up to standard (OMC 26-47).
Check: resurfacing alone comes to about $61M a year, against the $75M a year the city said in 2019-20 it needed for 250 lane-miles.
Lane counts and surfaces come from Public Works' own street inventory.

levels.label: Low
levels.text: Streets last longer: 80 years between rebuilds for local streets and 60 for arterials, resurfaced at the long end of the city engineer's range (20 years residential, 12 major).

levels.label: Typical
levels.text: 60 years between rebuilds for local streets and 50 for arterials, which carry more trucks; resurfaced in the middle of the city engineer's range (18 years residential, 10 major).

levels.label: High
levels.text: Streets wear out sooner: 50 years for local streets and 40 for arterials, resurfaced at the short end of the range (15 years residential, 8 major).

info.text: Full-depth reconstruction, all-in, for one foot of one lane.
Local: Omaha's 2026 bid for 183rd & Wright St was $1,599,850 for about 0.67 miles of two-lane concrete street, $226 a lane-foot. About 20% for design, inspection and contingency makes $270.
Minor arterial: the 2026 capital plan puts 84th St, Harrison to L, at $14.0M for 1.5 miles of five lanes, about $360 a lane-foot.
Collector, major arterial and freeway are estimates between and beyond those two.
Years between full rebuilds, with resurfacing in between. The input that moves the total most.

Well-maintained city streets average 50-60 years before reconstruction; timely overlays more than triple the life of a neglected one. Omaha still runs 1950s-70s concrete with panel repairs and overlays.
Mill and overlay, for asphalt and asphalt-over-concrete streets.
The 2025 resurfacing program was $28.6M for more than 150 lane-miles, about $191K a lane-mile or $37 a lane-foot, ramps and engineering included. 2020-2023 bond work averaged $265K a lane-mile.
Panel and joint repair: a concrete street's resurfacing.
A 2025 residential panel contract came to about $15 a lane-foot; 60th St came to about $61.
Years between resurfacings.
The city's maintenance engineer: 'fifteen to 20 years on a residential street... Major streets... 8 to 12 years'. Collector is between.

groups.title: Street upkeep
groups.what: What the city actually spends running streets day to day, from the 2026 adopted budget.
groups.how: The total is spread evenly over every lane-foot the city maintains, and each parcel pays for the lane-feet in front of it.

about.text: Each figure is a 2026 appropriation; the number in brackets is its budget organization.
Resurfacing programs are left out because they are already in pavement; so are design, inspection and administration, which are overhead on capital projects.
Sidewalks are not charged: abutting owners must repair them (OMC 26-41 to 26-44). The city's curb ramps are built with resurfacing, so they are in its cost.

info.text: Potholes, concrete panel replacement and crack sealing by city crews (116158).
Plowing, salt and brine (116154).
Street and right-of-way cleaning (116152).
Repair of the city's remaining brick streets (116122).
Traffic engineering: signal timing and repair, signs and pavement markings (116180).
OPPD owns and maintains most street lights and bills the city a yearly rate per light, which covers their replacement too (116200).
Routine bridge repair (116164). Replacement is under Bridges and signals.

groups.title: Bridges and signals
groups.what: 142 city-owned bridges and culverts (1.13M sq ft of deck) and 972 active traffic signals.
groups.how: Replacement cost divided by how long each lasts. Each is charged to the street it sits on; a signal goes to the biggest road at its intersection. With arterial sharing on, those on arterials are split across the city.

levels.label: Low
levels.text: Bridges last 100 years with rehabilitation; signals last 35 years.

levels.label: Typical
levels.text: FHWA's Nebraska bridge cost over a 75-year design life; a signalized intersection at $400K over 30 years, Omaha's median age at rebuild.

levels.label: High
levels.text: Bridges at the $530 a sq ft of Omaha's own viaduct projects; signals rebuilt every 25 years.

info.text: FHWA's 2025 replacement cost for Nebraska bridges off the National Highway System, 3-year average. Deck areas are FHWA's own.
City viaducts cost more: the capital plan's 42nd St and 72nd St bridges work out to $530-1,000 a sq ft, project costs included.
The 75-year design life AASHTO's bridge specification uses.
About $300K to rebuild an intersection in recent Midwest bids, plus about 30% for design and the city-supplied cabinet and controller.

params.label: Rebuild a pedestrian signal or beacon

info.text: Pedestrian signals, hybrid beacons and the like.
Omaha's own signals were rebuilt at a median age of 31 years.

groups.title: Sewer mains
groups.what: 2,819 miles of city-owned sanitary, storm and combined sewer main.
groups.how: Renewal per foot per year: part of the network is dug up and replaced, part is lined from inside, each divided by how long it lasts; plus the city's actual cleaning and repair spend, spread per foot. Mains 18 inches and smaller are charged to the lots along them, split by frontage like streets; wider mains and trunk lines are shared by sewer bill.

about.text: Mains wider than 18 inches drain a neighbourhood or a watershed rather than the block they run under, so they are shared like treatment.
Storm and sanitary mains are not told apart in the source layer, so both are counted.

levels.label: Low
levels.text: Three quarters of renewal is lining from inside, at a fraction of the cost of digging up the street; replaced pipe lasts 100 years, the top of Omaha's design manual range.

levels.label: Typical
levels.text: Half of renewal is lining and half is open-cut replacement; replaced pipe lasts 75 years, the middle of the design manual's 50-100.

levels.label: High
levels.text: Every main is dug up and replaced every 75 years; none is relined.

info.text: The share of renewal done by lining a pipe from inside (cured-in-place pipe) rather than digging it up. Omaha publishes no split.

Open-cut replacement costs a base amount plus an amount per inch of diameter. Phoenix's 2024 unit cost study puts it at $350-400 a foot for 8-inch, $770-940 for 24-inch and $1,230-1,550 for 36-inch, construction only. $150 + $35 an inch, about 20% above that for engineering, fits it: an 8-inch main comes to $430 a foot.
See Replacement, base: the two together give $430 a foot for 8-inch pipe and $990 for 24-inch.
Omaha's design manual gives gravity sewer 50-100 years.
Lawrence, KS paid $97.75 a foot to line 24-inch pipe in 2019, about $4 an inch, against $700-800 a foot to dig it up. $12 allows for small pipe costing more per inch, and for inflation.
Liners are commonly designed for about 50 years; some utilities expect much longer.
The 2026 Sewer Maintenance appropriation: cleaning and repair of mains, manholes and inlets (116511).

groups.title: Sewer plants and operations
groups.what: Two treatment plants, about 51 pump and lift stations, the CSO storage basin and force main, and running it all.
groups.how: Replacement value divided by life, plus yearly operating cost. These serve the whole sewershed, Bellevue, Papillion, La Vista, Ralston and others included, so only the city's share is charged: its sewer bills over what the system collects. Each parcel pays in proportion to its sewer bill.

about.text: Omaha publishes no replacement values for plants, pump stations or CSO works, so all three are estimates from capacity and other cities' costs.
For comparison, the sewer fund's own depreciation was $51.7M in FY2024 and $61.5M in FY2025, at what the assets originally cost rather than what they would cost now.

levels.label: Low
levels.text: Plants, pump stations and CSO works cost 20% less to replace than estimated, and last 50, 40 and 50 years.

levels.label: Typical
levels.text: $1.6B to replace the plants, over 40 years; $270M for pump stations, over 33; $260M for CSO works, over 42.

levels.label: High
levels.text: 25% more to replace than estimated, and shorter lives: 35, 25 and 35 years.

info.text: The two plants are being rebuilt to 46 and 95 million gallons a day at peak month, about 118 on an average day. Tomahawk Creek in Johnson County, KS cost $268M for 19 MGD in 2020; escalated and scaled for size, about $13.5M per MGD. 118 x $13.5M is about $1.6B.
A blend: structures about 50 years, equipment 20-25.
About 70 pumping stations less 19 flood-control ones. The nine big CSO lift stations at Omaha's own cost per MGD, the rest at about $2.5M each.
A blend of structures and pumps.

services.what: Allocated from the 2026 budget at the share property tax pays for: 21.9% of each General Fund line, plus the levies that are property tax outright.
services.how: Each line is spread over parcels by what drives it. They balance citywide by construction, so they change who pays more than their share but never the citywide gap. Edit config/budget.csv and rebuild to change them.

info.text: General Fund appropriations, or a levy rate in cents per $100 of assessed value for the debt, redevelopment and judgment funds.
General Fund lines x 21.9%, the share of the General Fund property tax pays for ($123.4M of $562.8M). Levy lines are the levy rate times $56.0B of assessed value.
People: residents plus employees, each employee counted as 0.4 of a resident. Residents: residents only. Per parcel: the same amount for every parcel.
Lines charged by street frontage are what property tax puts into streets today. They set the share of property tax credited to streets, and are not charged as services.

fixed.label: City property tax levy
